folake.notes: Your mother. Sells fabric at Balogun market and does the arithmetic in her head.

adebayo.notes: Your father. Civil servant. Paid late for eleven years and never once said so at home.

iyabo.notes: Your grandmother. Makes jollof over firewood and considers gas a personal insult.

okonkwo.notes: Your teacher. Sixty-three children in the class and she learned all their names.

chidi.notes: Your friend since primary school. Writes code, gets paid in a currency he cannot receive.

amaka.notes: Your sister. Two years younger, twice as decisive. Now a nurse in Leeds.

bello.notes: Stands at the road block. Has not been paid this month either.

nysc.notes: NYSC orientation camp. Shouts everything, including good news.

obi.notes: Your lecturer. Has been on strike four times in your degree and hates it.

nurse.notes: Public hospital. Knows exactly what is needed and exactly what is not there.

consular.notes: US consulate, Lagos. Ninety seconds. Has said no four hundred times this week.

recruiter.notes: London agency. Perfectly pleasant. Never says the word.

doyle.notes: Border officer. Says 'random' on every flight.

system.notes: Automated text: emails, bank messages, recorded announcements, printed forms.

nodes.title: Paying to be told no
nodes.sum: A visa fee buys consideration, not a visa, and it is not returned when the answer is no. Nigerians are refused at rates several times the global average, and the refused fees are a measurable national transfer to the refusing states.

nodes.title: Being cut to three months, single entry
nodes.sum: In July 2025 the United States reduced most non-immigrant visas for Nigerians to a single entry valid three months, replacing the five-year multiple-entry visas many held - and then suspended issuance entirely.

nodes.title: Meeting every requirement and being refused anyway
nodes.sum: The stated grounds are usually that the officer is not satisfied the applicant will leave. That is a prediction about the future, it cannot be disproved with documents, and it is not appealable in most categories.

nodes.title: The agent who filled in your form
nodes.sum: Where the process is opaque and the stakes are high, an industry of agents appears. Some are useful, many are extractive, and a few enter information the applicant has never seen - which the applicant is then held responsible for.

nodes.title: A passport that ranks 90th and shrinks
nodes.sum: The Nigerian passport reaches 44 destinations without a prior visa. The number has been falling, and the long-run trend is downward against peers.

nodes.title: The booklet that is not there
nodes.sum: Getting the passport at all is a hurdle before it is used. Booklets run short, the portal shows 'processing' for months, and the people who pay privately are served first.

nodes.title: Proving you are who you say, repeatedly
nodes.sum: Identity in Nigeria is assembled from several partial systems - NIN, BVN, voter card, driver's licence, certificate of origin - none of which is sufficient alone, and each of which requires the others.

nodes.title: Documents that are assumed to be forged
nodes.sum: Nigerian civil and academic documents attract verification demands that documents from other countries do not, at the applicant's cost and on the applicant's time.

nodes.title: The second room
nodes.sum: The brief asks about unusually high rates of random checks. The honest position: the mechanics are documented, the referral criteria are published in outline, and no government publishes a per-nationality secondary-inspection rate - so the disparity is attested by consistent reporting rather than by a statistic.

nodes.title: Deportation, and the third country
nodes.sum: Removal is not only to Nigeria. Third-country arrangements mean a Nigerian removed from one state may be delivered to another entirely.

nodes.title: Being the nationality the airline worries about
nodes.sum: Carriers bear fines for bringing inadmissible passengers, so they screen before departure - which moves part of the border to the check-in desk in Lagos.

nodes.title: The exit interview at your own departure
nodes.sum: Leaving Nigeria involves its own layers - immigration, security, sometimes a trafficking screening that is necessary in design and intrusive in execution, and which falls hardest on young women travelling alone.

nodes.title: Refused entry with valid documents
nodes.sum: A visa is permission to ask. Documented cases show Nigerians with valid visas, return tickets, accommodation and funds refused entry, detained for days, and removed - sometimes to a third country.

nodes.title: Refused for travelling without a man
nodes.sum: The clearest single intersection in this dataset: a state refused entry to hundreds of Nigerian women, not for anything about them, but because they arrived without a husband or male relative.

nodes.title: Coming home, and the desk at that end too
nodes.sum: Return is not frictionless either. Arrival in Nigeria involves its own informal costs, and for deportees and returnees a reception that is administrative rather than supportive.

nodes.title: Claiming asylum from a country nobody calls a war
nodes.sum: Nigeria is not at war in the way decision-makers picture, so a Nigerian claim starts from a presumption of safety and must dismantle it - which is a different and harder task than arriving from a recognised conflict.

nodes.title: Germany: refused, and deported to Italy
nodes.sum: The Dublin system means a Nigerian claim in Germany is frequently not decided on its merits at all, but declared inadmissible and routed to the first EU country of entry - and if that transfer fails, the clock restarts.

nodes.title: The years with no status and no exit
nodes.sum: Between refusal and removal there is a condition with no name: not lawful, not removable, not permitted to work, and not permitted to leave and return.

nodes.title: Regularising, and the fee that is the barrier
nodes.sum: Where a route to status exists, it is priced - and the price is set at a level that functions as the actual eligibility criterion.

nodes.title: Being read as a fraud before you speak
nodes.sum: No other nationality in this set of datasets carries a scam as its global shorthand. 'Nigerian prince' is a punchline in languages that have no other Nigerian referent, and it arrives in the room before the person does.

nodes.title: Yahoo boys, and the men who are not them
nodes.sum: The domestic term for internet fraudsters has become an international descriptor for young Nigerian men generally, including the overwhelming majority who are not involved.

nodes.title: Guilty until verified, at every institution
nodes.sum: The reputational default converts into procedure: more documents, more checks, longer holds, and a higher bar for the same transaction.

nodes.title: What it does to a person to be a punchline
nodes.sum: Distinct from the economic cost: the internal effect of belonging to a nationality that is a globally recognised joke about dishonesty.

nodes.title: Twenty years without PayPal
nodes.sum: From 2004 to 2026 Nigerians could not receive money through the world's default consumer payment platform. The exclusion was explicit, national, and outlasted the conditions given for it.

nodes.title: The card that stops working at the border
nodes.sum: About 120 million payment cards circulate in Nigeria and the overwhelming majority cannot be used abroad or online internationally - by design of the domestic rails and by bank-imposed ceilings.

nodes.title: Remittance in, difficulty out
nodes.sum: Money flows into Nigeria at scale and with official encouragement. Money flowing out, or being received by a Nigerian business from abroad, meets a different regime entirely.

nodes.title: Being de-risked as a category
nodes.sum: Compliance departments manage country risk by declining the country. The individual customer is never assessed, and never told that is what happened.

nodes.title: Being blocked for where your IP says you are
nodes.sum: Merchants and platforms exclude Nigeria at the network level. The block is national in scope, trivially evaded by the people it targets, and binding on everyone who is not trying to evade anything.

nodes.title: Platforms that flag you by default
nodes.sum: Freelance marketplaces, marketplaces and social platforms apply elevated scrutiny to Nigerian accounts, with suspension arriving before any explanation.

nodes.title: The internet costs more and works less
nodes.sum: Before any discrimination, the connection itself is expensive relative to income, unreliable, and dependent on the power supply in PWR-001.

nodes.title: Kidnapping as an industry
nodes.sum: What began as ideological abduction became a ransom business with a price list. It is low-risk, lucrative, and now operates across most of the country rather than one corner of it.

nodes.title: Taking the schoolchildren
nodes.sum: Mass school abduction became a repeatable tactic after 2014. The specific consequence is that education itself becomes a risk calculation, and it is calculated differently for daughters.

nodes.title: Being displaced inside your own country
nodes.sum: Millions have left home without crossing a border, which means no refugee status, no agency mandate, and frequently no camp - just another poor village absorbing people it cannot feed.

nodes.title: The security you have to buy
nodes.sum: Where the state does not provide protection, households and businesses purchase it - which makes safety an income-tiered product and leaves everyone else with the risk.

nodes.title: The checkpoint that wants twenty naira
nodes.sum: Routine police extortion is a small, constant, unavoidable levy on movement, and refusing it is more expensive than paying.

nodes.title: What happened at Lekki
nodes.sum: The clearest documented case of the state using lethal force on its own unarmed citizens in this dataset - established by a judicial panel, denied by the government, and unpunished.

nodes.title: Reporting a crime as a woman
nodes.sum: The institution that would record a sexual or domestic offence is frequently the one that dissuades, mocks, charges a fee, or suggests the family settle it.

nodes.title: The grid that goes off, nationally
nodes.sum: Not outages in the ordinary sense. The national grid collapses entirely, repeatedly, and everything downstream of electricity is built around the assumption that it will.

nodes.title: Paying for darkness
nodes.sum: More than half of registered electricity customers have no meter, so they are billed by estimate - and the estimates are systematically wrong in one direction.

nodes.title: The morning the fuel price doubled
nodes.sum: On 29 May 2023 the fuel subsidy was removed in a sentence, and the price of moving anything - people, food, goods - repriced within weeks.

nodes.title: Running a household at 34% inflation
nodes.sum: The management of a shrinking budget against rising prices is daily, skilled, unpaid work, and it is overwhelmingly done by women.

nodes.title: Being paid in a currency that is leaving
nodes.sum: Naira earnings against dollar-denominated costs - school fees abroad, software, medical treatment, imported goods - means a salary that falls in real terms without anyone cutting it.

nodes.title: A health system with a third of its doctors licensed elsewhere
nodes.sum: Nigeria trains health workers and then loses them, at a rate that has converted a staffing problem into a structural one.

nodes.title: Japa: the exit as a national event
nodes.sum: Emigration of skilled workers is not a trickle or an aspiration. It is measurable in the destination countries' own registration data, and the health sector is where it is most visible.

nodes.title: Being treated abroad, and being suspected there
nodes.sum: Nigerian patients and Nigerian-trained clinicians abroad both encounter a presumption - of health tourism in one direction, of inadequate training in the other.

nodes.title: One of the most dangerous places in the world to give birth
nodes.sum: Nigeria carries a share of global maternal deaths far out of proportion to its population, and the northern ratio is several times the national one.

nodes.title: Obstetric fistula: the injury of waiting too long
nodes.sum: Prolonged obstructed labour without a caesarean produces an injury that is preventable, repairable, and in Nigeria enormously common - and it ends the woman's social life as reliably as it damages her body.

nodes.title: Deciding whether to have a child at all
nodes.sum: Contraception, spacing and the number of pregnancies are frequently not the woman's decision to make, which converts every other maternal risk into a recurring one.

nodes.title: The cost of a delivery, in cash, on the night
nodes.sum: Facility delivery is priced and paid at the point of use, which makes the safest option the one that requires money to be available at 2am.

nodes.title: The bills that were rejected
nodes.sum: Nigeria's legislature has repeatedly declined to pass gender equality provisions. The refusals are recent, recorded, and are the reason several other issues in this dataset have no remedy.

nodes.title: Being an indigene of nowhere
nodes.sum: Indigeneship determines access to scholarships, state employment, quotas and land. It follows birth, not marriage - so a married woman is frequently treated as belonging to neither state.

nodes.title: Married before eighteen
nodes.sum: A third of Nigerian girls marry before 18, and in several northern states it is nearly two thirds. The constitutional provision that would have settled the age contains a clause that undoes it.

nodes.title: Inheriting, in theory
nodes.sum: The Supreme Court held in 2014 that customary law barring daughters from inheriting is unconstitutional. Twelve years on, most people affected have not heard of the judgment and compliance is very low.

nodes.title: Being a widow
nodes.sum: Widowhood in much of Nigeria triggers a set of practices that strip property, restrict movement and impose ritual humiliation - enforced by the husband's family and frequently by other women.

nodes.title: Cutting
nodes.sum: Female genital mutilation is prohibited by federal law that applies directly in one federal territory, prohibited by state law in thirteen states, and practised in the regions where prevalence is highest.

nodes.title: Whose body it is treated as
nodes.sum: Across marriage, health and inheritance law the recurring structure is that decisions about a woman's body are made with reference to a man's position.

nodes.title: Menstruation, and what it costs to manage
nodes.sum: Products, privacy, water and disposal are all purchased or absent, and where they are absent the consequence is measured in school days.

nodes.title: Being visible in public as a woman
nodes.sum: Street harassment, transport harassment and the assumption of availability are a continuous tax on moving through public space.

nodes.title: Benin City to Italy
nodes.sum: One city in Edo State became the main hub for sex trafficking between West Africa and Europe. The route is documented, the debt is priced, and the binding mechanism is an oath.

nodes.title: The Gulf contract
nodes.sum: Recruited legally as a housekeeper, flown out with a signed contract, and then unable to leave the country without the employer's permission. The brief calls this being sent somewhere and dumped; the legal name is kafala.

nodes.title: Knowing, and going anyway
nodes.sum: Awareness campaigns assume the women do not know. Many do. The decision is made against the alternatives available at home, and the alternatives are the rest of this dataset.

nodes.title: Being suspected of being trafficked
nodes.sum: The mirror of TRF-001: because the route is well documented, young Nigerian women travelling legitimately are screened, doubted and delayed on suspicion of being victims.

nodes.title: A university year that does not happen
nodes.sum: Public university teaching stops for months at a time. Students are not taught, not examined, not graduated, and not compensated.

nodes.title: The children who are not in school
nodes.sum: Nigeria holds one of the largest out-of-school populations in the world, and the majority of those children are girls.

nodes.title: A certificate that is discounted abroad
nodes.sum: Nigerian qualifications attract verification, equivalency downgrades and outright scepticism - a discount applied to the document rather than the holder.

nodes.title: NYSC, and a year the state assigns you
nodes.sum: The National Youth Service Corps posts graduates for a year to a state not of their choosing, and completion is required for much formal employment.

nodes.title: Sex for grades
nodes.sum: The transaction is well enough known to have a name, and it was documented on camera at two of the region's most prestigious universities.

nodes.title: The workplace version
nodes.sum: The same structure moves into employment: a man with discretion over hiring, confirmation, promotion or payment, and no functioning complaint route.

nodes.title: Being harassed and being the one who is judged
nodes.sum: Disclosure carries a reputational cost to the woman, which is why prevalence is understated everywhere including in this dataset.

nodes.title: The statistics that say there is no problem
nodes.sum: Nigeria's headline unemployment rate is around 4%, which is lower than Germany's. The number is not wrong; it is measuring something other than what people mean by unemployment.

nodes.title: Working informally, which is most people
nodes.sum: 93% of employment is informal, which means no contract, no pension, no sick pay, no maternity provision, and no mechanism when something goes wrong.

nodes.title: The name on the CV, abroad
nodes.sum: Before any question of qualifications, the name on the application changes the callback probability - which is one of the best-evidenced findings in labour economics.

nodes.title: What a woman's work is assumed to be
nodes.sum: High female self-employment and informality are read as entrepreneurial culture. They are the residue of exclusion from formal work.

nodes.title: A name the form cannot hold
nodes.sum: Nigerian names are long, tonal, frequently multi-part, and carry diacritics that systems strip. The result is a person whose documents do not agree with each other, through nobody's error.

nodes.title: The identity is frozen before you reach the airport
nodes.sum: Air travel locks a vetted identity at booking. A mismatch found later cannot be fixed at the desk by anyone, for technical reasons rather than unhelpfulness.

nodes.title: Sharing a name with somebody
nodes.sum: Name-based screening produces false positives, and clearing one is not a thing that can be done once.

nodes.title: The officer who decided, and the one who would not have
nodes.sum: A large share of the hurdles in this dataset are not policy. They are one person's decision on one day, which another person would have made differently, and which is then permanent.

nodes.title: The error that becomes your record
nodes.sum: A wrong date, spelling or status code entered once is copied forward by every later system, and the burden of disproving it is entirely the person's.

nodes.title: The file nobody can find
nodes.sum: Verification in Nigeria frequently depends on a physical record held by an institution with no functioning archive, and the absence is treated as the applicant's problem.

nodes.title: Being read as dishonest before you speak
nodes.sum: The brief asks for the psychological effects of being seen as bad. For Nigerians the content of the stereotype is specifically dishonesty, which means the suspicion attaches to the person's word rather than to their capability.

nodes.title: The relationship market, with the nationality priced in
nodes.sum: The brief names this directly. The identity changes who will partner with you, on what terms, and how the relationship is read by everyone around it - and the romance-scam association gives it a specific and unusually corrosive content.

nodes.title: Not being able to plan
nodes.sum: Currency movement, power failure, insecurity and administrative unpredictability together remove the assumption of continuity that any long project requires.

nodes.title: The arithmetic that never stops
nodes.sum: Running a household under ECO-002 is continuous mental computation - prices, credit, who is owed, what can wait - and it occupies the same capacity that would otherwise go to work or study.

nodes.title: The one who left, and the one who stayed
nodes.sum: Japa splits families into senders and receivers, and the remittance relationship carries obligation, guilt and quiet resentment in both directions.

nodes.title: What it takes out of the work
nodes.sum: The brief asks specifically about efficiency and growth. The costs are real, large, and attributed to the person rather than to the conditions in essentially every setting.

nodes.title: Back pain, and the fact that it is measured
nodes.sum: The brief asks about back pain specifically. It is not a figure of speech: Nigeria may carry one of the heaviest low back pain burdens in the world, and the rural figure is roughly double the urban one.

nodes.title: The stress of running a household, in the spine
nodes.sum: The single most directly relevant finding in this dataset to what the brief asked: Nigerian women who appraised their domestic responsibilities as very stressful had roughly three times the odds of low back pain.

nodes.title: Depression, arriving as a physical complaint
nodes.sum: Psychological distress in Nigeria commonly presents somatically, which means it is investigated as a physical problem, not found, and the patient is left believing nobody could identify what is wrong.

nodes.title: The productivity loss nobody has quantified
nodes.sum: The brief asks about effects on efficiency and growth. The honest position is that the components are well evidenced and the total is not, because the study joining them has not been done.

nodes.title: Proving who you are, again
nodes.sum: Every institution verifies you separately, none of them trust each other's verification, and each wants a different combination of documents you must locate, copy and produce in person.

nodes.title: The renewal treadmill
nodes.sum: Passport, licence, registration, insurance, membership, subscription, permit. Each has its own cycle and its own portal, so something is always about to lapse and the lapse is always your fault.

nodes.title: Open when you are at work
nodes.sum: Offices, clinics, banks and tradespeople operate during working hours, so accessing them costs annual leave or lost pay.

nodes.title: Hold music, and the person who cannot help you
nodes.sum: Support lines are built around cost per call. The person who answers can read the screen and rarely change what is on it.

nodes.title: The typo that becomes official
nodes.sum: One wrong character in a name, date, address or account number propagates into every system downstream, and correcting it is always harder than making it.

nodes.title: Their mistake, your problem
nodes.sum: Institutions presume their own records are correct. When they are not, discovering it, proving it and fixing it is entirely the work of the person harmed.

nodes.title: Mistaken for someone else
nodes.sum: Matching is fuzzy. A similar name, a shared birth date or a recycled phone number attaches another person's record - debts, fines, medical history - to you, and disproving it is your job.

nodes.title: After the crash
nodes.sum: The collision takes four seconds. What follows is months of insurers, assessors, hire cars, medical appointments and an argument about liability you did not want to have.

nodes.title: The ordinary injury
nodes.sum: A fall, a ladder, a kitchen, a football pitch, ice. The healing is the easy part; the hard part is doing your job and your life at reduced capacity while nobody adjusts anything.

nodes.title: You get ill, and nobody decided it
nodes.sum: Cancer, autoimmune disease, a cardiac event, a neurological condition. No behaviour reliably prevents them, no one is responsible, and the diagnosis reorganises everything around it.

nodes.title: The waiting list
nodes.sum: Where care is rationed by queue rather than price, the wait is assigned to you without negotiation and without a date you can plan around.

nodes.title: The illness generates an invoice
nodes.sum: In systems that bill individuals, a medical event produces a bill nobody quoted in advance, for an amount nobody can state beforehand, from providers you did not choose.

nodes.title: Cover attached to a job
nodes.sum: Where health cover comes through an employer, losing or changing work removes medical care at the same moment it removes income - and staying in a bad job becomes a medical decision.

nodes.title: The body slows on a timetable you do not set
nodes.sum: Recovery lengthens, sleep degrades, eyesight goes, strength declines. Gradual enough to be invisible, cumulative enough to be decisive, entirely non-negotiable.

nodes.title: Being burgled or robbed
nodes.sum: Someone decides to take your things. The loss is the smallest part; the aftermath is locksmiths, insurers, reference numbers, and not feeling right in your own rooms.

nodes.title: On the receiving end of someone else's driving
nodes.sum: Another person's speed, phone or inattention arrives in your life at a junction, and everything that follows is yours to administer.

nodes.title: Where you live decides which disaster you get
nodes.sum: Flood, wildfire, hurricane, earthquake, heatwave, freeze. The exposure comes with the ground, and the ground came with the job, the family or the price.

nodes.title: Someone is trying to defraud you, professionally
nodes.sum: Calls, texts, emails and messages engineered by people who do this full time, arriving whether or not you engage with anything.

nodes.title: Your data was lost by someone you never dealt with
nodes.sum: Organisations you have no relationship with hold records about you and lose them. Nothing you did caused it and nothing you can do fixes it.

nodes.title: The job ends because someone else did arithmetic
nodes.sum: Layoffs, restructures, acquisitions and closures arrive on a timetable set elsewhere. The decision is about headcount and cost centres, not about you, and the income stops anyway.

nodes.title: The manager you were assigned
nodes.sum: Whether a job is tolerable is largely one person, allocated to you, who can change without notice and without any change to your contract.

nodes.title: Working while ill, because the alternative is worse
nodes.sum: Where sick pay is thin or absent, illness becomes a financial calculation, and the calculation usually says go in.

nodes.title: Your largest expense is set annually by someone else
nodes.sum: For renters, the price of having somewhere to live is decided by another party once a year, and the only counter-move costs more than accepting it.

nodes.title: Things break, and they break together
nodes.sum: Boiler, roof, car, washing machine, phone. Each has a lifespan, they were often bought at the same time, and they fail at whatever moment they fail at.

nodes.title: Someone will need looking after
nodes.sum: An ageing parent, a sick partner, a child with additional needs. It arrives unscheduled, lasts years, is unpaid, and lands on whoever is nearest or least able to refuse.

nodes.title: Bereavement, and the paperwork of it
nodes.sum: Grief arrives with an administrative workload - registration, probate, accounts, utilities, pensions - executed by the person least able to concentrate.

nodes.title: Locked out of your own account
nodes.sum: Identity online is a chain of recovery methods. Break one link - a dead number, a lost authenticator, a closed email - and the chain does not reconnect.

nodes.title: The thing you relied on is discontinued
nodes.sum: Services close, formats are abandoned, apps are bought and shut, devices stop receiving updates. The decision is a company's; the migration is yours.

nodes.title: You must have a car, because of how the place was built
nodes.sum: Where there is no viable transit, car ownership is not a preference - it is a condition of employment, imposed by planning decisions made before you arrived.

nodes.title: The commute
nodes.sum: A daily journey is the largest recurring involuntary time cost most working people carry. It is unpaid, not counted as work, and mostly set by where housing is affordable.

nodes.title: The credential you must hold to be considered
nodes.sum: Employers set entry requirements. Roles that once needed a school certificate now need a degree, without a corresponding change in the work - so the qualification is a toll, not a choice.

nodes.title: The structures that made friends are removed
nodes.sum: School, university and early jobs supply repeated unplanned contact. Adult life does not, so friendship becomes something that must be organised or it ends.

nodes.title: You cannot afford to enforce your own rights
nodes.sum: Most everyday legal wrongs are worth less than the cost of pursuing them, so the right exists and the remedy does not - and the other party knows it.

nodes.title: Compelled participation
nodes.sum: Jury service, tax filing, census, registration, court witness summons. Duties that take real time, are not optional, and are scheduled by the state.

nodes.title: Everything you have requires upkeep
nodes.sum: Possessions, accounts, documents, health and qualifications all decay without input. The work returns you to baseline; none of it is progress.

nodes.title: The queue
nodes.sum: Waiting is allocated to you by whoever is providing the thing, in units they do not pay for and you cannot spend elsewhere.

nodes.title: You were born into a cohort and the cohort has a price
nodes.sum: House prices, interest rates, the labour market in your graduation year, whether a pandemic falls in your twenties. None is chosen, and all of it compounds.

nodes.title: The volume of small compulsory decisions
nodes.sum: Tariffs, plans, policies, renewals and options all require comparison. The choosing is imposed; the alternative is paying the default price.

nodes.title: Ambient activation that never resolves
nodes.sum: News, notifications and always-on messaging produce a baseline of alertness nobody opted into, and it does not switch off because the devices do not.

SC-LAGOS-STREET.note: A main road in Lagos: danfo buses, generators outside every shop, traders on the median.

SC-GENERATOR-YARD.note: The compound at night when the grid goes. Where the family sits and where the generator is started.

SC-NYSC-CAMP.note: NYSC orientation camp: the year the state assigns you, in khaki, on a parade ground.

SC-ROAD-BLOCK.note: The police checkpoint on the expressway that wants twenty naira and will take an hour if it does not get it.

SC-CLASSROOM-NG.note: NG variant of SC-CLASSROOM. A nigerian public primary classroom, sixty wooden desks packed wall to wall, a cracked blackboard, louvred windows, no fans turning.

SC-HOME-DAY-NG.note: NG variant of SC-HOME-DAY. The parlour of a lagos flat in daylight, velvet-covered settee under plastic, a standing fan, louvre windows, a wall clock.

SC-HOME-NIGHT-NG.note: NG variant of SC-HOME-NIGHT. The parlour of a lagos flat at night lit by one bulb on an extension lead, a generator audible outside, moths at the window.

SC-DESK-NIGHT-NG.note: NG variant of SC-DESK-NIGHT. A cluttered desk at night in lagos, laptop glow, an inverter and cables, a phone charging.

SC-OFFICE-NG.note: NG variant of SC-OFFICE. A lagos fintech office, desks close together, an inverter humming, a whiteboard, blinds against the glare.

SC-CAMPUS-NG.note: NG variant of SC-CAMPUS. A nigerian federal university campus, concrete faculty blocks, a noticeboard thick with paper, palms, students' bikes.

SC-CONSULATE-NG.note: NG variant of SC-CONSULATE. The us consulate waiting area in lagos, bolted seating, numbered windows behind thick glass, a ticket display.

SC-AIRPORT-NG.note: NG variant of SC-AIRPORT. Murtala muhammed airport departures hall, check-in queues behind barriers, trolleys, a currency board.

SC-AIRPORT-SEC-NG.note: NG variant of SC-AIRPORT-SEC. An airport secondary screening room, bolted chairs, a counter, a clock, a door with a small window.

start.text: Surulere, Lagos. A flat on the second floor with a standing fan that works when the power does.
You are being born. You will not remember it, and it is the most dangerous year you will ever survive.
He's here. Adebayo. He's here.
Your mother is Folake. She sells fabric at Balogun market and does her accounts in her head faster than anyone with a calculator.

options.text: I open my eyes.
options.note: there is nothing else you can do

options.text: I cry until somebody comes.
options.note: it works; it will keep working for about two years

eyes.text: Ceiling fan, still. A face. The face is enormous and it is laughing and crying at the same time.

cry.text: Somebody comes immediately. This is the last time in your life that asking will work this well.

out.text: You survive the first year, in a country where that is a real achievement and is never once asked for on a form.

start.text: Your grandmother makes jollof over firewood in the yard, because she says gas has no smoke and smoke is the point.
The rice at the bottom of the pot goes slightly burnt. That part is fought over by everyone including the adults.
Come and stir, {player}. Both hands.

options.text: I stir it with both hands.
I ask why we don't use the gas cooker.

why.text: Because your generation eats rice that tastes of nothing and calls it food.

stir.text: The pot is bigger than you. Your arms ache. The smoke gets in your eyes and you refuse to move.
Good. Now you know how to do it. Nobody can charge you for it later.

options.text: I ask for the bottom part.
I wait to be given some.

bottom.text: You get the burnt rice at the bottom. Your sister Amaka negotiates for half of it and gets a third.
Nothing about today required anything from anyone in an office.

the-teacher-who-decided.title: The teacher who decided you were clever

start.text: Sixty-three children in the class. Mrs Okonkwo knows every name, which you will only later understand was a decision she made.
Who can tell me what this word means?

options.text: I put my hand up.
options.note: you are not certain you are right

options.text: I say nothing and hope she asks me.

hand.text: You are right. She does not make a fuss of it, which is why you remember it.

wait.text: She asks you. She had already decided to.

after.text: She gives you a book that is too old for you and tells you to bring it back when you have finished it, not before.

options.text: I promise to bring it back.
I ask if there are more like it.

more.text: There are thousands. That is the problem and it is also the good news.

keep.text: You'll do something. Make sure it's something you chose.
Nine seconds of an adult's attention. It will hold for twenty years.

start.text: You are doing homework when the light goes. Not your building - the street, then the district.
Nigeria's national grid does not dim. It collapses, completely, and has done so repeatedly - a total system failure that takes everything off at once.
Gen. {player}, bring the jerry can.

options.text: I bring the jerry can.
I ask how long it will be off.

howlong.text: Nobody knows. That is not a thing that gets announced.

gen.text: The generator starts on the fourth pull. It is loud enough that the family stops talking and starts shouting instead.
It burns about 1,200 naira of petrol an hour. Your father runs it for two hours a night, which is a decision about money disguised as a decision about bedtime.

options.text: I do my homework by the generator.
I ask why we pay the electricity bill at all.

bill.text: Estimated billing. They estimate what you used, and you pay it. Whether or not there was light.

work.text: You finish your homework. The generator goes off at ten and the silence afterwards is enormous.
Every business on your street owns one of these. That cost is inside the price of everything any of them sells.

start.text: The street is the pitch. The goals are a gutter and somebody's gate. A car coming is a stoppage in play and nothing else.
{player}, you're in goal. You're always in goal.

options.text: I go in goal.
I refuse and demand to play up front.

goal.text: You let in five. Nobody keeps score properly. Chidi celebrates one of them for a full minute.

front.text: You play up front, score once off your shin, and describe it afterwards as a volley.

dusk.text: I'm going to write software. Get paid in dollars. From here.

options.text: I tell him he'd be good at it.
I ask how you get paid in dollars from here.

how.text: That's the part I haven't figured out.
He has identified, at fifteen, the exact problem that will take up the next ten years of his life.

end_scene.text: It gets dark fast, the way it does here. The streetlight does not come on, because it never has.

start.text: The suya spot is a drum grill, a table, and a man with a knife who has been doing this at the same corner for nineteen years.
Beef on sticks, dusted with yaji - a spice mix of ground groundnut, chilli and ginger - wrapped in newspaper with raw onion and tomato on top.

options.text: I order and wait by the grill.
I ask for extra yaji.

extra.text: He looks at you, decides you can take it, and gives you an amount that suggests he has misjudged.

wait.text: You eat it standing up, at eleven at night, with Chidi arguing about a football match that finished four hours ago.
{player}, this is the best thing in the entire country and it costs two hundred naira.

options.text: I agree completely.
I say the country has other good things.

other.text: You name four. He concedes one of them.

out.text: Nobody asked for anything. Nothing had to be approved. Remember that it did not.

twenty-naira-at-the-road-block.title: The checkpoint that wants twenty naira

start.text: Your father is driving you back from your aunt's. There is a plank across one lane, two oil drums, and three officers.
This is not a border or a crime scene. It is a stretch of public road where a toll is collected that is not a toll.
Oga. Wetin you carry?

options.text: I watch my father hand over the money.
I ask, quietly, what we did wrong.

pay.text: Twenty naira, folded small, passed low, taken without either man looking at the other's face. The whole thing takes four seconds and both of them have done it a thousand times.

options.text: I ask what happens if you refuse.
I say nothing until we have driven away.

refuse.text: Then it is a two-hour search of a car with nothing in it. Or your tail light is suddenly broken. Twenty naira is the cheap option and they know it.

away.text: Three more before home. Sixty naira. Your father budgets for it the way other people budget for petrol.
You are fifteen. You have just learned that the cheapest way through is to pay, and that everyone knowing this is what keeps it working.

the-year-that-does-not-happen.title: ASUU, and a degree that takes six years

start.text: You are in your third year of a four-year engineering degree at a federal university.
ASUU - the Academic Staff Union of Universities, the lecturers' union - has gone on strike. Lectures stop. The campus does not close; it simply has nothing happening on it.
Go home, {player}. Don't come back until you hear. I don't know when you'll hear.

options.text: I ask how long these usually last.
I ask what the strike is about.

howlong.text: The last one was eight months. The one before that, five. I have been on strike four times since you started.

about.text: Salaries that arrive late, and a funding agreement the government signed and did not honour. It is the same dispute every time.

home.text: You go home. The strike lasts eight months. Nothing is refunded, nothing is compressed, and the academic year is simply added to the end of your life.

options.text: I get a job for the eight months.
I study alone and keep the habit.
I lose the eight months entirely.

job.text: You work in a cyber cafe. It pays badly and teaches you more about computers than the third year would have.

study.text: You keep the habit. Two of your friends do not, and one of them never comes back to finish.

lost.text: Eight months. You are not lazy; there is simply nothing to be diligent at, and that turns out to be corrosive in a way you did not expect.

out.text: You graduate in six years and two months. Every employer abroad will read that as a gap you have to explain.

the-year-the-state-assigns-you.title: NYSC: a year, in khaki, wherever you are sent

start.text: You have graduated. Before you may take a proper job, you must complete NYSC - the National Youth Service Corps.
It is one year. The federal government assigns you to a state, usually not your own, usually far. You wear khaki. You are paid an allowance that does not cover the year.
Your posting is on the board! If your name is on the board, it is final!

options.text: I go and look for my name.
I ask whether a posting can be changed.

change.text: Redeployment is on medical or marital grounds. Do you have either?

board.text: The board is a sheet of A4 with names printed small. You find {document}, misspelled the way it has been misspelled all your life, next to the name of a state eleven hours away by road.

options.text: I accept it.
I ask why nobody is posted to their own state.

why.text: National unity! That is the purpose of the scheme!
It is the stated purpose, and it is a real one. It is also why you will spend a year somewhere you cannot afford to travel back from at Christmas.

accept.text: You serve the year. Without the certificate at the end of it, most formal employers in the country will not consider you at all - so the year is not optional in any way that matters.

start.text: The announcement is one sentence long and is made during a speech: the fuel subsidy is gone.
Petrol roughly triples within days. In a country where nearly everything moves by road and nearly every business runs a generator, that is not a fuel price. It is the price of everything.
The fabric didn't change. The transport changed. So the fabric changed.

options.text: I ask how much more the bus is.
I ask what she'll do about the stall.

bus.text: The danfo fare to work doubles in a week. Over a month that is most of what you were saving.

stall.text: Raise prices and lose customers, or keep prices and lose money. That is the whole choice.

adjust.text: Everyone adjusts. Portions get smaller. The generator runs one hour instead of two. Nobody calls it a crisis because it does not arrive on one day.

options.text: I start sending money home monthly.
I move closer to work to kill the transport cost.

send.text: You send what you can. It becomes a fixed cost of being yourself.

move.text: You move into a smaller place nearer the office. The rent is a year in advance, in cash, which is how it is done.

out.text: Inflation runs above thirty per cent. Your salary is a number that does not change while everything it buys does.

twenty-years-without-paypal.title: Paid in a currency you cannot receive

start.text: Chidi did it. He writes software, and a company in Berlin wants to pay him four thousand dollars for three months' work.

The problem is not the work. The problem is that for most of two decades PayPal did not let Nigerian accounts receive money - you could send, not receive - and much of the internet's freelance plumbing runs through exactly that kind of service.
They asked for my PayPal. I had to explain. You can hear them start to wonder about you.

options.text: I ask what he uses instead.
I ask why it is like that.

why.text: Fraud rates, sanctions-screening costs, and the fact that it is cheaper for a payments company to exclude a country than to assess the people in it one at a time.

instead.text: A friend's account in the UK. He takes a cut. Or crypto, and then explaining to my bank where it came from.
Both of those look, to a compliance system, exactly like what someone doing something wrong would do. So the workaround produces the suspicion that justified the exclusion.

options.text: I tell him to use my aunt's account.
I ask what happens if the bank asks questions.

aunt.text: He uses your aunt's account in Leeds. She takes nothing, which somehow makes the favour heavier.

bank.text: Your account has been restricted pending review. Please visit a branch with identification.
It takes nine days and two visits. Nothing was wrong. Nothing is apologised for.

out.text: He gets paid, eventually, minus about eleven per cent lost to the arrangement of getting paid at all.

yahoo-boys-and-the-men-who-are-not.title: Being the category before being the person

start.text: You have a job at a Lagos fintech. It is a good job. You are good at it.
A vendor call with a firm in London. Cameras on. You introduce yourself and there is a pause of about half a second that you have learned to recognise.
Sorry - and you're based where, exactly?

options.text: I say Lagos.
I say I'm based with the company.

deflect.text: They ask again, more precisely. There is no version of this conversation in which the answer does not come out.

lagos.text: Nothing is said. The meeting continues. Afterwards the contract requires a UK-registered intermediary to hold the funds, which was not in the draft.
It's the 419 thing. Every one of us pays for it and none of us did it.

options.text: I ask whether it is worth objecting.
I ask how he handles it.

object.text: You could object. It would be accurate, and it would make you the difficult vendor, and the contract is worth more than the point.

handle.text: I get ahead of it. I explain before they ask. It works, and I hate that it works.

out.text: A small number of people ran an email fraud famous enough to have a number. Two hundred million people carry the presumption it created, at every counter, for the rest of their lives.

start.text: You apply for your first Nigerian passport at thirty. The booklet costs 35,000 naira and the appointment system has been fully booked for weeks.
You get one through a cousin who knows someone, which is not corruption exactly and is not nothing either.
Look at you, {player}. A traveller.

options.text: I open it and read every page.
I put it somewhere safe immediately.

read.text: Photograph, dates, a number. The name inside is {document}, because that is what the records say and has said since you were four days old.
Nobody ever showed you the moment it was written down wrong. There was no scene. It was simply always like this.
Remember this: {document} is the ENGLISH name you have forever. Every visa application and every border officer will read it, and you will answer to it.

safe.text: It goes in the metal box with the certificates and the deeds to your grandmother's land.

out.text: Today it is a passport and you are a person who could go somewhere. That feeling is real. Keep it.

a-passport-that-opens-less.title: What the booklet is actually worth

start.text: Amaka is planning her wedding trip and has asked you to look up which countries you could all go to without applying in advance.
You find the passport rankings. The Nigerian passport sits near the bottom of the global table - visa-free access to a few dozen places, most of them in West Africa.

options.text: I check what a British passport gets.
I look for somewhere we can actually all go.

compare.text: Around one hundred and ninety destinations, without asking anyone. The difference is not effort or money. It is the cover of the book.

somewhere.text: You settle on Ghana, which needs nothing, and is genuinely lovely, and was not the first choice of a single person in the family.
It's fine. It's actually fine. I just wanted to see snow once.

options.text: I tell her we'll do snow another year.
I start looking at what a Schengen application needs.

snow.text: You say another year. You will say it three more times.

schengen.text: Bank statements for six months, proof of employment, proof of accommodation, travel insurance, a fee that is not refunded, and an appointment slot that does not exist until it suddenly does.

out.text: Everybody has a passport. Not everybody has the same passport.

the-security-you-have-to-buy.title: Paying privately for what the state does not provide

start.text: The estate holds a meeting about security. There have been two break-ins on the next street.
The arrangement proposed is standard: a levy per household for two gatemen, a boom barrier, and lights at the junction.
{player}, everyone pays. If two houses don't pay, the whole thing collapses.

options.text: I pay the levy.
I ask what the police do.

police.text: They come after. If you can fuel their vehicle.
Police units are often expected to be facilitated by the complainant - fuel, transport, sometimes paper - which quietly converts public protection into a thing you buy.

pay.text: You pay the levy, and for the generator, and for water because the mains is unreliable, and school fees because the public schools near you are not a real option.

options.text: I add it all up.
I decide not to add it up.

total.text: Security, power, water, school. You are paying twice for four things: once in tax, once again in cash, and only the second payment produces anything.

nototal.text: You do not add it up. Most people do not. It is easier to carry as four separate annoyances than as one number.

out.text: This is what people mean when they say the state is absent. Not that it does nothing - that you replace it, privately, at your own expense, and are still taxed.

start.text: Amaka's wedding. Four hundred guests, a colour scheme that was non-negotiable, and aso-ebi - the matching fabric everyone on the family's side wears - chosen by your mother from her own stall.
There is a live band, jollof in industrial quantities, and an MC who will not stop talking over the music.
Stand up straight. Everybody is looking at this family today.

options.text: I dance badly and publicly.
I spray money at the couple like everyone else.

dance.text: You are terrible. Your grandmother, who is ninety-one, is better, and everyone films it.

spray.text: Notes, one at a time, onto the couple's foreheads while they dance. It looks like excess and is actually a public accounting of who showed up.

amaka.text: {player}, I got the NHS job. Leeds. We go in March.

options.text: I tell her I'm happy for her.
I ask if she's sure.

sure.text: There are three of us on a ward that needs eleven. I'm not leaving because I hate it. I'm leaving because I can't do it.

happy.text: Nigeria trains nurses and doctors who then work elsewhere - a large share of them licensed abroad. People call it japa: to flee, to escape.
Tonight it is a wedding, and your sister is happy, and both things are true.

start.text: You are applying for jobs in the UK. Forty-one applications, two replies, both automated.
Chidi suggests an experiment. Send the identical CV twice: once as {document}, once with your middle name, which is English, and a UK mobile number.

options.text: I try it.
options.note: it feels like cheating and it is not

options.text: I refuse to do it.

refuse.text: You refuse for six more weeks. Then you try it.

try.text: The second version gets three responses in nine days. Same experience, same degree, same person.
Now you know, {player}. The question is what you do with knowing.

options.text: I use the English name from now on.
I keep my own name and accept the cost.
I ask whether this is even provable.

prove.text: In the aggregate, yes - matched-CV studies have measured exactly this for decades. In your own case, never. No individual rejection ever says why, and that is what makes it survivable for the people doing it.

use.text: You use the English name. You get an interview. You spend the first ten minutes of it being quietly furious and the rest performing calm.

keep.text: You keep your name. It costs you an unknown number of interviews that you will never be able to count, which is its own particular kind of weight.

out.text: Either way, the arithmetic was done before anybody read a word you wrote.

start.text: There is a conference in Atlanta and your employer will pay for everything. You need a US visitor visa.
You file the DS-160 - the United States non-immigrant visa application - and pay the fee of 185 dollars. It is not refundable, whatever the outcome. The next interview slot is in five months.
On the day you queue from 5am with your employment letter, bank statements, the conference invitation and your father's land documents, because someone said property helps.
Good morning. What is the purpose of your travel?

options.text: I explain the conference carefully.
I hand over the invitation letter.

letter.text: I don't need documents. Just answer the questions.

explain.text: What do you do? Are you married? Do you have children?
The whole interview lasts about ninety seconds. He is typing before you finish the third answer.

options.text: I mention I'll be back for my sister's wedding.
I answer exactly what is asked and nothing more.

wedding.text: It is true and it is the strongest thing you have. He does not write it down.

slip.text: I'm sorry, I'm not able to approve your application today.

He passes a printed slip through the slot. It cites section 214(b): the applicant did not demonstrate strong enough ties to their home country to overcome the presumption that they intend to immigrate.

options.text: I ask which tie was not strong enough.
I take the slip and go.

which.text: The decision is at the officer's discretion. You may apply again.

Every applicant is presumed to be an intending immigrant until they prove otherwise. You cannot appeal it. You may reapply, pay again, wait five months again, and be assessed by whoever is at the window that morning.

out.text: The fee is gone. The conference happens without you. Your employer is understanding in a way that is worse than being angry.

start.text: Second attempt, different country. You have a UK visa this time, properly issued, and a conference in Manchester.
At the desk the officer takes your passport, looks at it longer than he looked at the two before you, and picks up a phone.
Just a few more questions, sir. This way.

options.text: I ask if there's a problem.
I follow him.

room.text: A room with fixed chairs and a window onto the corridor. Four other people are waiting. You notice, and are ashamed of noticing, that you all look roughly the same.
Your bag is searched. Your phone is taken to another room and brought back. Nobody tells you how long any of it will be.

options.text: I ask how long this will take.
I wait without asking.
I ask whether I can call my employer.

wait.text: Two hours and forty minutes. Then the passport comes back, stamped, with no explanation offered and none owed.

options.text: I ask what that was about.
I say thank you, and hate myself for it.

what.text: He has already turned away. There is no form for this, no record you can request, and nothing that happened to you today is anywhere in writing.

out.text: You make the conference on the second day. You give a good talk. You do not mention any of this to anyone there.

refused-entry-with-valid-documents.title: A visa is permission to ask

start.text: A year later. A different trip, a valid visa, a return ticket, a hotel booking and an invitation letter.
{document}. Step aside, please.

options.text: I ask what the issue is.
I step aside.

aside.text: Here is the thing nobody explains before you travel: a visa is permission to travel to the border and ask to enter. The decision itself is made at the border, by the officer in front of you, and it is not appealable there.
You were refused a US visa in 2019. Why?

options.text: I explain what 214(b) means.
I say they never told me.

explain.text: You explain it accurately. Explaining a refusal fluently is itself read as the behaviour of someone who has thought about refusals a great deal.

decide.text: Four hours. Then a decision, delivered standing up, in a corridor.
I'm not satisfied you're coming for the reason you've given. You'll be returned on the next available flight.

options.text: I ask to speak to someone more senior.
I ask what happens to my visa.
I say nothing at all.

visa.text: A refusal of entry is recorded. It will be visible to the next country you apply to, and to the one after that, and you will be asked to explain it every time for the rest of your life.

out.text: You fly home the same night, in the same clothes, having been inside the country for eleven hours without leaving the building.
